faq.q: What is the difference between moment of inertia and mass?
faq.a: Mass is the amount of matter an object has. Moment of inertia depends on mass and how that mass is distributed relative to the axis.
asks: Is I just mass times distance?
Does I depend on the shape?

faq.q: When do I use the parallel axis theorem?
faq.a: You use it when you know the moment of inertia about an axis through the center of mass, but you need it for a parallel axis.
asks: What if the new axis is not parallel?
Does the distance 'd' have to be perpendicular?

faq.q: What does the perpendicular axis theorem tell me?
faq.a: It tells you that for a flat object, the moment of inertia about an axis perpendicular to the plane equals the sum of the moments about the two axes in the plane.
asks: Does this only work for flat objects?
Is it always Ix plus Iy?

faq.q: Do I need to calculate the moment of inertia for every object?
faq.a: No, you only need to calculate it if the standard formula is not given or if you are moving the axis.
asks: Can I just use the formula for a circle?
Is there a general formula for everything?

faq.q: What are the units for moment of inertia?
faq.a: The unit for moment of inertia is mass times distance squared, which is kilograms times meters squared.

facts: Moment of inertia depends on mass and the distribution of mass.
The parallel axis theorem relates I about two parallel axes.
The perpendicular axis theorem applies to planar objects.
The formula I = m d^2 shows the dependence on distance squared.

quiz.say: A rod of mass m and length L rotates about its center. What is its moment of inertia?
quiz.why: The formula for a rod rotating about its center of mass is m times L squared divided by twelve.

wrong.0: This formula is typically used for a solid disk, not a rod.
wrong.2: This is the moment of inertia when rotating about one end, not the center.
wrong.3: This calculation misses the necessary squaring of the distance term.

quiz.say: A thin ring of mass m and radius r rotates about its center. What is I?
quiz.why: For a thin ring, every particle is at radius r, so the moment of inertia is simply m times r squared.

wrong.0: The moment of inertia must have units of mass times distance squared.
wrong.2: This value is closer to the moment of inertia of a solid disk.
wrong.3: The formula requires the square of the radius, not just the radius.

quiz.say: Using the parallel axis theorem, if a disk has Icm and we move the axis distance d away, what is the new I?
quiz.why: The theorem states the new moment is the original moment plus the mass times the distance squared.

wrong.1: You should add the terms, not multiply them together.
wrong.2: You must include the mass 'm' in the second term of the addition.
wrong.3: The relationship is additive, not involving division.
